concepts.gloss: The more basic and the information-packaged construction used to convey comparable content, when both counterparts are acceptable.
A packaging alternation with different quantifier/negative scope and thus potentially different truth conditions.

rules.concept: truth-condition differences from scope-sensitive information packaging
rules.statement: Although canonical and information-packaged alternatives normally describe the same truth conditions, differences in the relative scope of a quantifier such as many and clausal negation can change their truth conditions.
rules.condition: When comparing a basic clause with a passive, existential, or complement-preposing alternative that changes the relative structural positions of many and not, check whether many takes scope over negation or negation takes scope over many; do not infer semantic equivalence merely because the information-packaging relation is present.

contrast.text: Many instructors were not at the seminar. [many > not: a large number were absent]
There were not many instructors at the seminar. [not > many: the number present was small]
Leila didn't assess many of the proposals. [negation can have wide scope over many]
Many of the proposals weren't assessed by Leila. [many has wide scope over the negation]
I haven't greeted many of those neighbours. [ordinary object position]
Many of those neighbours I haven't greeted. [preposed object; relative scope may differ]

rules.concept: left and right dislocation as information-packaging constructions
rules.statement: Left and right dislocation are distinct information-packaging patterns in which material linked to a clause appears at the left or right edge, respectively, instead of occupying the corresponding ordinary clause position.
rules.condition: For a clause with a detached NP and an associated clause containing a coreferential pronoun, classify the construction as left dislocation when the NP precedes the clause and right dislocation when the NP follows it; compare with an ordinary undislocated counterpart.

contrast.text: Those tickets, they sold out yesterday. [left dislocation]
They sold out yesterday, those tickets. [right dislocation]
Those tickets sold out yesterday. [ordinary counterpart]
My neighbour, she has already left. [left dislocation]
She's already left, my neighbour. [right dislocation]

rules.concept: subject–dependent inversion contrasted with subject–auxiliary inversion
rules.statement: Subject–dependent inversion places a non-subject dependent such as a locative complement before the verb, with the subject following the verb; this is distinct from subject–auxiliary inversion where a finite auxiliary precedes the subject.
rules.condition: When a clause shows inversion, distinguish the order preposed dependent + verb + subject from auxiliary + subject + other predication material, and reserve the unqualified information-packaging term inversion in this chapter for subject–dependent inversion.

contrast.text: On the mantelpiece stood two porcelain figures. [subject–dependent inversion]
Two porcelain figures stood on the mantelpiece. [canonical order]
Were two porcelain figures on the mantelpiece? [subject–auxiliary inversion]
Inside the courtyard were three visitors. [subject–dependent inversion]
Were three visitors inside the courtyard? [subject–auxiliary inversion]

rules.concept: compatibility and combination of information-packaging constructions
rules.statement: Different information-packaging constructions can occur together in a clause when their structural requirements are compatible, but some pairs cannot be combined; existential formation and subject extraposition are mutually incompatible under the constructions described here.
rules.condition: For a candidate clause with more than one information-packaging construction, identify each pattern separately and test whether its required subject and clause structure coexist: preposing plus right dislocation, cleft plus extraposition, or passive plus extraposition may combine, while the defined existential and subject-extraposition constructions demand incompatible structures.

contrast.text: That draft she endorsed, the committee chair. [complement preposing plus right dislocation]
It was at midnight that it became clear the signal was lost. [it-cleft plus extraposition]
It was anticipated by the advisers that the decision would be delayed. [passive plus extraposition]
There was an unexpected delay at the station. [existential construction]
It is obvious that the station was closed. [subject extraposition]
The pianist it was who was congratulated by the judges. [preposing, cleft, passive; marked but interpretable]

rules.concept: clause labels versus information-packaging construction names
rules.statement: Certain information-packaging labels name clause types as well as constructions (passive, existential, cleft), whereas others name only the construction (preposing, postposing, extraposition, dislocation): the clause should instead be described as having a preposed or extraposed constituent.
rules.condition: When describing a non-canonical clause, reserve passive clause, existential clause or cleft clause for the recognised clause-level categories; for preposing, postposing, extraposition and dislocation identify the construction and the relevant constituent or position rather than inventing a new clause-type label such as preposing clause.

contrast.text: The portrait was restored by Isla. [passive clause; passive construction]
There are several lamps in the corridor. [existential clause; existential construction]
It was Isla who restored the portrait. [cleft clause; cleft construction]
That portrait Isla restored last week. [clause with a preposed object]
It was unfortunate that the doors closed early. [clause with an extraposed subject]
